Ericsson has meanwhile absorbed the reputational and financial consequences of the United States Department of Justice proceedings tied to corruption in Iraq — a matter that constrained its American expansion and thinned executive bandwidth through the mid-2020s. Nokia has not been free of governance strain — its own profit warnings in 2023 triggered a significant share sell-off — but it entered the Hotard era without the legal cloud that shadowed Stockholm. On the 5G front, Dell'Oro Group data placed Nokia and Ericsson within a few percentage points of each other in Western RAN market share through 2024, with Samsung closing ground in North America and South Korea.

## Cisco: The Routing Incumbent

In service-provider IP routing, Cisco's dominance is structural. Its IOS XR operating system runs on the ASR 9000 and NCS platforms that anchor backbone and peering infrastructure across most of the world's largest telcos. Nokia inherited, via the January 2016 Alcatel-Lucent acquisition, a credible challenger in the 7750 Service Router family and its SR OS platform. That heritage gave Nokia a foothold in carrier core routing that no other European vendor possesses.

The competitive tension has sharpened as data centre fabric and carrier core routing converge. Nokia's SR Linux — an open, container-native network operating system built from scratch — sits at the centre of its hyperscaler and AI data centre pitch. Where Cisco's NX-OS and its Nexus switching portfolio dominate legacy enterprise and carrier data centre fabric, Nokia's proposition is that SR Linux's programmability and its native integration with telemetry and automation toolchains make it better suited for AI training cluster networking, where east-west traffic volumes dwarf anything classical spine-leaf designs were engineered for.

Cisco's scale advantage — revenues in the high-USD 50 billion range through fiscal 2025, against Nokia's €22-23 billion envelope — is formidable. But Cisco's routing revenue has faced pressure from the same AI-driven shift that Hotard is exploiting: hyperscalers building custom silicon and white-box switching are eroding Cisco's data centre margin profile, creating space for software-forward challengers willing to run on merchant silicon.

## Juniper and the HPE Variable

Juniper Networks — the service-provider router vendor that the MX Series placed as Nokia's closest direct competitor in carrier IP/MPLS — is now mid-absorption into Hewlett Packard Enterprise. The deal, announced in January 2023 and cleared by the European Commission and US Department of Justice after extended review, closed in 2024. The integration has occupied Juniper's commercial and engineering leadership through most of the period when Nokia was integrating Infinera and repositioning toward AI data centres.

For Nokia, the Juniper-HPE combination is a double-edged development. On one hand, an absorbed Juniper may accelerate in enterprise distribution, a channel Nokia has historically underserved; HPE's Aruba networking business could pull Juniper intelligence toward campus and branch, dimming its carrier focus. On the other hand, HPE's balance sheet and procurement relationships with hyperscalers could accelerate Juniper's own data centre ambitions. The outcome remains unresolved within the frozen window.

| Vendor | Primary Segment | 2024 Revenue (approx.) | IP/Optical Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nokia | Telco + AI DC (emerging) | €22–23bn | Full stack: IP routing, optical, fixed, submarine |
| Ericsson | Telco RAN + managed services | SEK ~250–260bn (~€22bn) | Minimal routing/optical |
| Cisco | Enterprise + carrier networking | USD ~57bn | Dominant in routing; optical via Acacia |
| Juniper/HPE | Carrier + enterprise routing | USD ~5–6bn (standalone) | Service-provider routing, growing DC |
| Arista | Cloud/AI data centre | USD ~7–8bn | DC switching dominant; limited carrier |
| Huawei | Full telco stack | CNY ~700bn (~€88bn) | Full stack; restricted in West |

## Arista: The Data Centre Incumbent Nokia Must Displace

If Ericsson is Nokia's equal-weight adversary in radio, Arista Networks is the dominant force Nokia must challenge if the AI data centre routing thesis is to pay out. Arista's EOS — the single-image operating system that runs across its entire switch and router portfolio — has made it the default fabric vendor for hyperscalers, cloud-native enterprises, and, since 2022, for the GPU cluster networks that underpin AI training at scale. Microsoft, Meta, and major cloud providers are Arista reference customers.

Nokia's SR Linux competes on programmability, disaggregation, and openness. Its partnership with Microsoft — reported in industry coverage through 2024 and 2025 as Nokia engaged Azure infrastructure teams on IP fabric deployments — was the clearest early signal that the SR Linux platform was earning hyperscaler credence. But Arista's installed base, its deep EOS automation ecosystem, and its gross margin profile (historically above 60 percent) reflect a product-market fit that Nokia has not yet matched at scale in the data centre layer.

Hotard's competitive edge here is architectural: Nokia can offer a coherent IP-over-optical stack — 7750 SR routers feeding directly into Nokia's WDM optical transport, now dramatically expanded by Infinera's ICE6 and ICE-X coherent optics platforms — that Arista cannot replicate. Arista sells Ethernet switching. Nokia, post-Infinera, can sell the switching layer and the photonic layer in a single commercial relationship, which matters to hyperscalers seeking to compress the number of infrastructure vendors operating inside their campuses and long-haul corridors.

## Huawei: The Constrained Giant

Huawei's total revenues — spanning devices, carrier networks, enterprise, and cloud — dwarf every Western peer. Its telecom equipment division alone is a formidable competitor in Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America, where Nokia and Ericsson face a well-capitalised rival operating at Chinese-domestic cost structures. Huawei's optical transport and IP routing portfolios are technically mature; its OXC and OptiXtrans platforms compete directly with Nokia's optical equipment in markets where Huawei is permitted to operate.

In the West, Huawei's operational footprint has been systematically reduced since 2019. The UK's Telecoms Security Act, the US NDAA Section 889 restrictions, and equivalent legislation across Five Eyes and European Union member states have effectively closed the most lucrative carrier markets to new Huawei deployments. Nokia has been a direct beneficiary — rip-and-replace contracts in the United Kingdom and Germany, in particular, have transferred legacy Huawei network positions to Nokia and Ericsson at scale. The restriction also insulates Nokia's SR Linux data centre pitch from Huawei's CloudEngine switch portfolio in North American and European hyperscaler campuses.

## Nokia Technologies: The Licensing Moat

None of Nokia's named competitors — not Ericsson, not Cisco, not Arista — can match the Nokia Technologies patent licensing income stream. Nokia's portfolio of cellular standard-essential patents, assembled through decades of mobile research and the Alcatel-Lucent and Bell Labs heritage, generates recurring royalty income from smartphone manufacturers and, increasingly, automotive and IoT device makers. This licensing segment contributed approximately €1.1–1.2 billion in annual net sales through the early 2020s, at operating margins substantially above the group average.

The licensing income is structurally different from product revenue: it scales with global device shipments rather than capital expenditure cycles, it survives telco capex droughts that compress equipment margins, and it funds research investment that feeds back into next-generation standards work. Ericsson has a comparable but smaller licensing unit; Cisco, Juniper, and Arista have no equivalent. In downturns — and Nokia endured a severe one through 2023 and early 2024 as North American carrier spending contracted — Nokia Technologies served as a margin buffer that pure-play equipment vendors lacked.

## The Integrated Stack as Differentiator

The argument Hotard inherited, and which he has sharpened toward AI data centre audiences, is that Nokia's breadth is itself a competitive weapon. An Arista-only data centre vendor must source optical transport from Ciena or Coherent. A Cisco-dominant carrier must layer in third-party optical. Nokia's post-Infinera stack — SR Linux fabric, 7750 SR routers, PSE-4 and PSE-V custom photonic silicon, Infinera ICE-X coherent modules, and Nokia Wavelength Routing Mesh — offers a single-vendor coherent IP-optical architecture from server rack to intercontinental submarine cable.

> "We have a unique combination of IP and optical that others simply can't replicate," Hotard said at the Nokia Capital Markets Day in late 2025, framing the integrated portfolio as the primary basis for differentiation in AI data centre fabric bids.

Whether the integration discount that markets have historically applied to diversified telecom vendors converts to an integration premium in an AI infrastructure cycle — where hyperscalers place enormous value on operational simplicity and single-vendor accountability — is the central competitive bet of the Hotard era. The field against which that bet plays out, from Ericsson's radio dominance to Arista's data centre hegemony to Cisco's routing incumbency, is formidable. Nokia's edges — optical scale from Infinera, Alcatel-Lucent's IP routing pedigree, the patent licensing cushion, and the Western market shelter from Huawei — are real. Whether they compound into durable market share gains remains the open question of 2026 and beyond.

chapters.title: From 2016 Alcatel-Lucent through Lundmark, Infinera, Hotard
chapters.body:
## The Alcatel-Lucent Inheritance

The January 2016 close of Nokia's acquisition of Alcatel-Lucent — agreed in April 2015 for approximately €13.4 billion (~$15.6 billion) — was arguably the most consequential strategic transaction in Finnish telecommunications history since the company's own pivot from rubber and cables to handsets a generation earlier. [Nokia press release, April 2015](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)

What Alcatel-Lucent brought to the merged entity was not primarily the struggling handset operations Nokia had already shed to Microsoft in 2014. It was the IP Networks routing portfolio — the Alcatel-Lucent 7750 Service Router lineage, the Bell Labs optical transmission heritage, and the subsea cable systems business — that would, a decade later, become the architecture from which Justin Hotard would attempt to build a position in the AI data centre infrastructure market.

The deal rationale at the time was framed primarily around 5G network convergence. Nokia's then-CEO Rajeev Suri argued that the combined entity could deliver end-to-end network infrastructure from radio access to core, providing Nokia a scale and portfolio breadth to compete with Ericsson and the ascending Chinese vendors. The €900 million (~$960 million) annual synergy target within three years anchored the financial case.

Bell Labs, Alcatel-Lucent's research arm, was retained rather than stripped — a decision that preserved the IP Networks routing and optical networks R&D pipeline that would subsequently produce the FP5 network processor silicon central to Nokia's SR Linux data centre router positioning.

## The Lundmark Restructuring, 2020–2025

Pekka Lundmark arrived at Nokia's Espoo headquarters in August 2020 as successor to Suri, who had led the company since 2014. Lundmark, previously chief executive of Fortum, the Finnish energy utility, inherited a company that had stumbled in the early 5G deployment wave — losing share to Ericsson and facing margin compression — and a revenue base that would peak approaching €25 billion during the post-COVID 5G spending surge before beginning a sustained contraction.

| Year | Revenue (€B) | YoY Change |
|------|-------------|------------|
| 2020 | 21.9 | — |
| 2021 | 22.2 | +1.4% |
| 2022 | 24.9 | +12.2% |
| 2023 | 22.3 | −10.4% |
| 2024 | 19.7 | −11.7% |

*Sources: [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000924613](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000924613)*

Lundmark's central strategic move was a declared R&D investment acceleration, directing capital back into the 5G radio and network silicon programmes that had fallen behind under Suri's later tenure. The restructuring, which included reductions of roughly ten thousand employees over 2020–2022, was framed as freeing capital for technology reinvestment rather than straightforward cost reduction. The multi-year operational framework Lundmark established — with CFO Marco Wirén, who joined from Wärtsilä in January 2021 — set the financial architecture against which the Infinera deal and the Hotard succession were subsequently layered.

By late 2024, as carrier capital expenditure cycles moderated globally and the 5G peak subsided, Nokia's annual revenue had compressed to approximately €19.7 billion (~$21 billion) — down roughly 21 per cent from the 2022 peak. The structural challenge was visible: Mobile Networks, historically the largest segment, faced pricing pressure and a customer mix increasingly weighted toward cost-sensitive tier-two operators as Tier 1 US carriers completed their initial 5G rollouts.

The Network Infrastructure segment — the Alcatel-Lucent-heritage franchise spanning IP Networks routing, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, and Submarine Networks, led by Federico Guillen since January 2023 — was by late 2024 the business group in which Nokia's next strategic chapter would have to be written.

## The Infinera Transaction

In June 2024, Nokia announced it had agreed to acquire Infinera Corporation, the Santa Clara-based optical networking equipment vendor, for approximately $2.3 billion in a combined cash and all-stock transaction. [Nokia announcement, June 2024](https://www.nokia.com/investors/) The deal represented the most significant optical networking M&A move since Nokia-Alcatel-Lucent itself.

Infinera brought a design-led optical systems capability based in California, a Latin American carrier customer base that complemented Nokia's existing European and Asian footprint, and — critically — hyperscaler optical transport customer relationships that Nokia's internal optical business had not established at comparable depth. The PSM-series coherent optical systems and the Infinera engineering organisation represented genuine additions to the Nokia portfolio rather than a consolidation play.

The transaction closed February 28, 2025 — thirty-three days before Justin Hotard formally assumed the CEO role. The timing was not incidental: the Infinera integration was structured as a foundational piece of the incoming CEO's strategic platform rather than a legacy transaction to be managed around. The combined Optical Networks entity substantially scaled Nokia's presence in the hyperscaler optical infrastructure market — precisely the customer segment Hotard would subsequently address with the IP Networks routing portfolio.

## The Hotard Succession

Justin Hotard's appointment as President and Chief Executive Officer, effective April 1, 2025, represented a deliberate break from the Scandinavian-industrial CEO succession pattern that had characterised Nokia since Jorma Ollila. Hotard arrived from Intel Corporation, where he had served as Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Data Center and AI Group — the division responsible for Intel's Xeon server, Gaudi AI accelerator, and data centre networking portfolios. Before Intel, he had led the High Performance Computing and AI business at Hewlett Packard Enterprise.

The profile was explicitly AI-data-centre-native. Nokia's board under Chair Sari Baldauf — herself a former Nokia EVP of Networks from the pre-smartphone era — had reached into the hyperscaler supply chain executive cohort rather than the telecom equipment industry for the succession. Hotard's Iowa State industrial engineering pedigree, combined with a Kellogg MBA and multi-decade Intel and HPE operating experience, produced an operating identity formed inside the AI infrastructure ecosystem.

The strategic signal embedded in the succession was direct. Nokia's IP Networks routing portfolio — SR Linux running on FP5 silicon, a platform capable of operating as a data centre spine router in the Clos fabric architectures that hyperscalers and AI cloud builders deploy at scale — had been generating early commercial momentum with hyperscaler customers including Microsoft. The board concluded that a CEO whose operating identity was shaped inside the AI infrastructure ecosystem was the appropriate succession choice for a company attempting to establish durable position against Arista Networks, Cisco Systems, and Juniper Networks in data centre routing.

## Forward Catalysts

The strategic agenda under Hotard as of the frozen snapshot date converged on three operational milestones that would define Nokia's competitive trajectory through 2026.

The first was the Infinera integration timeline. The February 2025 close initiated a multi-quarter process of customer base rationalisation, supply chain consolidation, and product portfolio integration across Nokia's legacy Optical Networks business and Infinera's PSM-series coherent optical systems. The hyperscaler optical transport relationships acquired through Infinera were the primary near-term revenue expansion opportunity — and the pace of integration execution would determine whether those relationships deepened or eroded to competitors.

The second was the AI data centre router commercial programme. Nokia's SR Linux platform on FP5 silicon entered the AI data centre routing market as a challenger to Arista's EOS-on-Ethernet installed base and Cisco's Nexus franchise. The Microsoft engagement — representing a reference-quality hyperscaler validation — was the central commercial milestone. Quarterly order progression in the data centre router category under Guillen's Network Infrastructure group was, by early 2026, the most closely watched near-term financial signal at Nokia.

The third was Hotard's capital allocation posture toward Network Infrastructure relative to Mobile Networks. The revenue compression in the carrier-facing Mobile Networks segment provided both the financial pressure and the strategic rationale for accelerating the AI data centre pivot. How Hotard calibrated R&D spend between the two largest business groups — and whether Network Infrastructure's margin profile could absorb the investment required to win hyperscaler router contracts at scale against incumbents with decades of installed base — was the defining medium-term strategic question.

Nokia's competitive position through 2026 would be substantially determined by whether the Alcatel-Lucent routing heritage, the Infinera optical acquisition, and the Hotard AI-data-centre strategic mandate cohered into a commercial programme capable of generating durable revenue growth. The Lundmark era had stabilised the operational and financial foundation. The Infinera transaction had scaled the optical footprint. The question Hotard's tenure would answer was whether a Finnish telecommunications equipment vendor, through a chain of acquisitions from Bell Labs to Infinera, had assembled the pieces to take a meaningful share of the infrastructure spend underpinning the AI buildout.

chapters.title: 5G IP, IP Networks SR Linux, Optical Networks technology, Bell Labs
chapters.body:
## The Alcatel-Lucent Inheritance

Nokia's technology depth in IP routing and optical transport is overwhelmingly an Alcatel-Lucent inheritance. When Nokia closed the €15.6 billion (~$16.6 billion) acquisition in January 2016, it absorbed two formidable engineering traditions: the Bell System research culture embedded in Bell Labs, and the Service Router lineage that Alcatel had built after its own 2006 merger with Lucent Technologies. A decade on, that inheritance — augmented by the February 2025 Infinera close and reoriented under Justin Hotard's data-centre mandate — defines what Nokia brings to the AI infrastructure buildout.

## SR Linux and the Data Centre Router Opportunity

The most consequential platform Nokia produced in the Lundmark era is SR Linux, a cloud-native network operating system launched in 2020 as a deliberate break from the proprietary software model the company had maintained since the 7750 Service Router family first shipped in the mid-2000s. SR Linux runs as containerised microservices, exposes a fully programmable, model-driven interface via gNMI and gRPC, and was designed from the ground up for hyperscaler workflows — specifically for engineering teams that deploy infrastructure through GitOps pipelines rather than CLI sessions.

The platform runs on Nokia's 7250 IXR (Interconnect Router) family, powered by Nokia's fifth-generation FP5 forwarding processor. FP5 — designed in-house at Nokia's Ottawa silicon team — delivers line-rate programmable forwarding with integrated telemetry and was specifically architected to handle the east-west traffic patterns of AI training clusters, where hundreds of GPU servers exchange gradient updates in tightly scheduled all-reduce collectives. That distinction matters: traditional service-provider routers optimise for north-south subscriber flows; the AI data centre requires routers that can sustain terabit-scale, low-latency mesh topologies with deterministic jitter and congestion-aware load balancing.

The hyperscaler validation Nokia secured through 2023 and 2024 included Microsoft Azure, which deployed Nokia's IP routing fabric within Azure data-centre interconnect infrastructure, as reported by [Light Reading](https://www.lightreading.com). Nokia distinguished itself from incumbent data-centre switch vendors by offering a fully open NOS that operators could extend through standard YANG models and Python-based event-handler scripts — a posture that resonated with hyperscaler teams accustomed to running their own network automation stacks.

On Nokia's Q4 2024 earnings call, Pekka Lundmark framed the strategic logic:

> "AI is driving a fundamental rethinking of what network infrastructure needs to do. IP Networks is extremely well positioned. We have the products, we have the customers, and we are winning."

When Justin Hotard assumed the CEO chair on April 1, 2025, he sharpened the message. Arriving from Intel's Data Center and AI Group, where he had led product strategy sold directly into the same hyperscaler accounts Nokia was courting, Hotard signalled that SR Linux would be treated not as a niche routing win but as a platform business requiring a dedicated go-to-market motion:

> "Nokia has the routing technology that the AI data centre needs. My job is to make sure we're having the right conversations at the right level inside these customers — and that we're building the services and software layer that makes Nokia a strategic partner, not just a vendor."

## 5G Transport: The Mobile Backhaul and Fronthaul Stack

SR Linux's data-centre trajectory does not displace Nokia's foundational role as the IP transport layer for 5G mobile networks. The company's 7705 SAR (Service Aggregation Router) and 7750 SR families carry the backhaul and midhaul traffic connecting 5G radio units, distributed units, and centralised units across the F1, F2, and NG interfaces that define Open RAN and disaggregated 5G architectures.

Nokia's Mobile Networks business group contributed roughly 40% of group net sales through the mid-2020s, and the routing equipment that IP Networks supplies to 5G operators created a durable bundling dynamic: carriers deploying Nokia's AirScale ReefShark SoC radios tended to purchase the Nokia IP transport stack for its timing-synchronisation compatibility (IEEE 1588v2 / SyncE) and native segment-routing support (SR-MPLS and SRv6). That cross-business dependency supported IP Networks' margin through the initial 5G rollout cycle but also exposed Nokia to mobile capex fluctuations.

By 2025, with North American and European Tier 1 operators having largely completed initial 5G NR macro deployments, the incremental growth narrative within IP Networks had shifted decisively toward the data centre — precisely the rotation Hotard's mandate was constructed to capture.

## Optical Networks: The Infinera Augmentation

Before Infinera, Nokia's optical portfolio traced to Alcatel's 1830 Photonic Service Switch (PSS) platform and to successive generations of coherent DSP silicon — the PSE-3, PSE-3s, and PSE-V — developed by Nokia's Lannion, France engineering team. The PSE-V delivered up to 1.2 Tb/s per wavelength in coherent transmission, competitive with market-leading Ciena and Infinera products.

The February 28, 2025 Infinera close — at approximately $2.3 billion (€2.1 billion) in cash and stock — added three capabilities Nokia could not replicate organically on a reasonable timeline. First, Infinera's ICE6 coherent DSP architecture, developed at the company's San Jose engineering centre, brought a vertically integrated chip-to-subsystem design methodology that reduced per-bit transmission cost at 800G spectral efficiency and positioned Nokia for the 1.6T generation via the forthcoming ICE7. Second, Infinera's GX Series open line system platforms had achieved strong penetration in North American Tier 1 carriers and cable operators — a segment Nokia's Lannion team had not consistently accessed. Third, Infinera's submarine cable management software, inherited from Coriant (which Infinera itself acquired in 2018), deepened Nokia's Submarine Networks business group beyond its historical Alcatel Submarine Networks cable-laying and installation focus.

| Optical asset | Origin | Core capability |
|---|---|---|
| 1830 PSS platform | Alcatel heritage | Metro and long-haul DWDM switching |
| PSE-V coherent DSP | Nokia Lannion | 1.2 Tb/s per wavelength |
| ICE6 coherent DSP | Infinera San Jose | 800G, open pluggable |
| GX Series open line | Infinera | NA Tier 1 and cable penetration |
| Submarine NMS | Coriant / Infinera | End-to-end submarine cable management |

The combined optical portfolio placed Nokia in direct competition with Ciena Corporation across all three major optical segments: long-haul DWDM, metro coherent, and submarine.

## Nokia Bell Labs

Bell Labs remains the most symbolically significant asset Nokia holds. Founded as Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1925 and the birthplace of the transistor (1947), information theory (Claude Shannon, 1948), Unix, and the C programming language, the institution arrived at Nokia through Alcatel-Lucent and has been maintained at its Murray Hill, New Jersey campus as an active research organisation.

Under Nokia's stewardship, Bell Labs concentrated its long-horizon work on three clusters: future network architectures, including 6G air-interface research contributing to the 3GPP Release 20 standardisation cycle; applied AI for network operations, autonomous network management, and energy minimisation; and quantum networking, specifically quantum key distribution (QKD) for carrier-grade cryptographic applications. The institution publishes in *Nature*, *Science*, and top-tier IEEE venues, and holds thousands of active patents — a stock that complements rather than duplicates the broader Nokia licensing portfolio.

The institutional credibility of Bell Labs functions as a recruitment and partnership instrument that Nokia's principal competitors — Ericsson, which dismantled its own research lab infrastructure through successive restructurings; and Cisco, which absorbed Bell Labs-era talent but never held the brand — cannot readily replicate.

## Patent Portfolio and Nokia Technologies

Nokia Technologies, the fourth business group and the one with no hardware product line, operates as a pure patent licensing entity. Nokia is one of the five largest declared holders of 5G Standard Essential Patents (SEPs) globally, alongside Ericsson, Huawei, Qualcomm, and Samsung, according to declarations filed at the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI). The portfolio spans 2G through 5G NR radio, video and audio codec technologies, and internet protocol standards.

Nokia Technologies' licensing revenues ran in the range of €1.3–1.5 billion (~$1.4–1.6 billion) annually through the early 2020s, providing a structurally high-margin, capital-light contribution to group free cash flow that underpinned Nokia's capacity to fund the Infinera acquisition and sustain the FP5 silicon and coherent DSP investment cycles simultaneously. Long-term bilateral agreements with Apple, Samsung, and the broader smartphone and IoT device ecosystem anchor the revenue base; while headline disputes with individual licensees surface periodically in court filings, the underlying portfolio has proven durable across multiple licensing renewal cycles.

Nokia's SEP standing in 3GPP and IEEE standardisation bodies also carries strategic value beyond licensing economics: it gives Nokia's engineering teams direct influence over whether SR Linux's SRv6 extensions, Bell Labs' 6G proposals, or Infinera's coherent optics interoperability specifications become the industry baseline — an upstream leverage point that pure-hardware competitors without comparable standards participation cannot access.

chapters.title: Telecom cycle, Ericsson competition, AI cycle, Huawei dynamics, patent licensing
chapters.body:
## A Cycle That Gave and Then Took Away

The revenue chart tells the clearest version of the first risk. Nokia's top line rose from €21.9 billion in 2020 to a post-COVID peak of €24.9 billion in 2022, carried by a wave of global 5G capital expenditure that rewarded every vendor with a credible radio access network portfolio. Then the wave broke. By 2023 revenue had compressed to €22.3 billion; by 2024 it had fallen further to €19.7 billion (roughly $21 billion), a decline of more than 20 per cent in two years from peak. [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)

The mechanism was straightforward. North American carriers — AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile — had front-loaded 5G buildout ahead of spectrum auction schedules and then pulled back sharply once initial coverage obligations were met and balance sheets required repair. Indian operators, briefly the most enthusiastic spenders in the world following Reliance Jio's 5G launch, likewise settled into a maintenance rather than expansion posture by mid-2024. European operators, perpetually squeezed between regulatory fragmentation and low average revenue per user, never generated the capex intensity that the upgrade cycle implied.

The risk Nokia carried into 2025 and beyond was that the next telecom capex cycle — driven by whatever combination of Open RAN densification, fixed wireless access, and 6G preparation emerges — could be both smaller in absolute terms and more distributed in vendor share than the 5G wave it follows. For a company whose Mobile Networks segment remained structurally exposed to carrier budgeting decisions, the historical pattern offered limited comfort.

## The Nordic Rival and the Korean Disruptor

Within that compressed carrier market, Nokia faced intensifying competition from its closest peer. Ericsson, also headquartered in the Nordic region and also rebuilt on a decade of restructuring, had stabilised its own finances and regained commercial aggression in the Radio Access Network market. [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/) The two companies had effectively divided the global 5G vendor landscape among themselves and Samsung Networks wherever Huawei and ZTE were restricted — but that oligopoly structure provided only partial protection.

Samsung Networks was the more disruptive competitive threat in the medium term. The South Korean conglomerate had demonstrated in the United States — most visibly through its Dish Network and T-Mobile contracts — that its integrated semiconductor-to-software-to-antenna architecture could deliver competitive performance at aggressive price points. As more operators began re-architecting networks with Open RAN-compliant interfaces, Samsung's willingness to subsidise market entry with hardware margin compression posed a direct challenge to Nokia's installed base in key accounts.

The financial stakes were significant. Mobile Networks accounted for a substantial share of Nokia's overall revenue, and the segment's margins were already under pressure from the volume declines of 2023 and 2024. Any further share loss to Ericsson in Europe or Samsung in Asia-Pacific and North America would compound the cycle headwind with a structural one.

## The Hyperscaler Bet and Its Inherent Uncertainty

Justin Hotard arrived on April 1 2025 carrying the strategic narrative that Nokia's IP Networks segment — the Alcatel-Lucent-inherited routing portfolio built around the SR Linux platform — was positioned to capture a share of AI data centre interconnect spending. The logic was coherent: hyperscalers building out massive GPU clusters required high-bandwidth, low-latency fabric routing at a scale that traditional telecom router vendors had not served, and Nokia's SR Linux architecture offered programmability features that resonated with the software-defined infrastructure preferences of Microsoft, Google, and Amazon.

The opportunity was real. The uncertainty was equally real. Nokia was entering a market where Arista Networks had built a dominant position in data centre switching and where Cisco's position in enterprise and service provider routing gave it enormous incumbency advantages. Juniper Networks — acquired by Hewlett Packard Enterprise in a deal that closed in early 2024 — brought its own AI data centre ambitions backed by a much larger distribution channel. And Nvidia, through its Spectrum-X Ethernet networking platform, was actively competing for the GPU cluster interconnect budget that Hotard had identified as Nokia's target.

The competitive landscape Nokia was entering in AI data centre routing was arguably more difficult than the carrier market it was trying to diversify away from. Carrier markets were oligopolistic, relationship-driven, and multi-year in contract structure. Hyperscaler infrastructure procurement was faster-moving, more technically demanding, and populated by buyers who had the engineering sophistication to evaluate claims rigorously and the financial scale to negotiate aggressively on price. Nokia's reported Microsoft engagement in SR Linux was encouraging, but a single early hyperscaler relationship did not constitute a business line.

## Huawei: Restrictions That Could Narrow or Reverse

The geopolitical dimension of Nokia's competitive environment was embodied most directly in Huawei. The Chinese vendor's exclusion from 5G deployments across the United Kingdom, Sweden, and several other European markets had benefited Nokia and Ericsson over the preceding four years — but that exclusion was never a permanent condition and was subject to shifting diplomatic currents between Brussels, Washington, and Beijing.

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, Huawei remained restricted in core network functions across most Western markets, but the enforcement landscape had become more complicated. Some European operators had sought extensions to rip-and-replace timelines on cost grounds. Sovereign exemptions for certain network layers had been negotiated in specific jurisdictions. And in markets across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and sub-Saharan Africa — where Nokia competed vigorously for carrier contracts — Huawei faced no restrictions at all and competed with the full weight of Chinese state-backed vendor financing behind it.

The risk ran in both directions. A material relaxation of Huawei restrictions in Europe would directly threaten Mobile Networks revenue. A tightening of restrictions in markets where Nokia currently competed on commercially neutral terms could provide upside — but could equally trigger retaliatory Chinese procurement policies that disadvantaged Nokia in markets where it had significant presence.

## Patent Licensing: High-Margin, High-Stakes Renewals

Nokia Technologies, the group's patent licensing arm, contributed revenue that was disproportionately profitable relative to its absolute size. The portfolio — built over decades of research investment in fundamental wireless communications standards — generated licensing income from handset manufacturers and other companies practising cellular standards globally. [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)

The business model was structurally sound but periodically exposed to litigation and renewal risk. Major licensing agreements with large handset manufacturers were negotiated on multi-year cycles, and the renegotiation of any significant agreement carried the risk of either revenue reduction or costly arbitration. Nokia had navigated several such disputes historically, including prolonged litigation with Apple in the 2010s that ultimately resolved in Nokia's favour and produced a substantial licensing settlement.

The forward risk was that the composition of the handset industry continued to evolve in ways that complicated licensing. The rise of Chinese original equipment manufacturers — Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo — as the dominant volume players in global smartphone shipments created counterparties with different negotiating postures and greater willingness to litigate in multiple jurisdictions simultaneously. Any significant gap in licensing coverage from a major manufacturer would fall directly to Nokia's bottom line.

## The Execution Challenge of the Hotard Succession

The sixth and perhaps most immediate risk entering 2025 was the simplest to state and the hardest to quantify. Justin Hotard had spent his career inside the semiconductor and data centre infrastructure world — most recently as Executive Vice President and General Manager of Intel's Data Center and AI Group. Nokia was a different kind of company: a European telecommunications equipment vendor with a unionised Finnish workforce, a decades-deep carrier customer network, and a cultural inheritance from both its own history and the Alcatel-Lucent integration that remained visible in its organisational structure.

Pekka Lundmark had spent his tenure from August 2020 through March 2025 restructuring Nokia's cost base, narrowing its strategic focus, and restoring operating credibility after the turbulence of the Rajeev Suri era's failed diversification. The result was a leaner company — but also one whose identity and customer relationships were built around telecommunications. Hotard's strategic repositioning toward AI data centre infrastructure, however logical from a secular growth perspective, required Nokia to develop new customer relationships, new sales motions, and new engineering credibilities in a market where it was not yet a known quantity.

Transition risk was real in the leadership layer below the CEO as well. Any significant departure from the executive team assembled under Lundmark — particularly from the Network Infrastructure or Mobile Networks leadership who carried the carrier relationship capital — would represent a setback to the continuity of commercial execution even as the strategic direction changed. The market would be watching Hotard's first full year of results with particular attention to whether AI data centre routing traction was appearing in reported numbers alongside, rather than substituting for, stable carrier revenue.

chapters.title: Hotard era execution, Infinera integration, AI data centre routing
chapters.body:
## The Intel alumnus inherits a compressed revenue line

When Justin Hotard walked into Nokia's Espoo headquarters as chief executive on April 1, 2025, he became the first CEO in the company's modern telecommunications era to arrive from outside the industry's traditional radio-access and core-network supply chain. His prior mandate — running Intel Corporation's Data Center and AI Group — was a deliberate signal from Nokia's board. The company that had spent the first half of the 2020s methodically executing Pekka Lundmark's network-technology modernisation was pivoting toward a second act: positioning itself as infrastructure supplier to the AI hyperscale build-out.

The backdrop was sobering. Nokia's full-year 2024 revenue stood at €19.7 billion (approximately $21 billion), down sharply from the €24.9 billion peak recorded in 2022 as operator capital expenditure tracked the height of the 5G deployment cycle. In the two years that followed, carrier spending moderated across North America, Europe and Asia, compressing the Mobile Networks segment that had been the principal engine of Lundmark's tenure. The task handed to Hotard was not merely to arrest that decline but to locate and develop a new growth vector capable of sustaining Nokia's standing as Europe's dominant telecommunications equipment group.

## Infinera integration and the optical networks expansion

The single most consequential asset Hotard inherited was still being assembled when he arrived. Nokia had announced its all-stock-and-cash acquisition of Infinera Corporation in June 2024 for approximately $2.3 billion and closed the transaction on February 28, 2025 — thirty-one days before Hotard's first day in the chair. The combination materially changed the shape of Nokia's Optical Networks segment.

Infinera brought a silicon photonics vertical-integration capability, an installed base concentrated among Tier 1 North American carriers and — critically for Nokia's AI data centre thesis — a set of established hyperscaler relationships in the United States. The optical interconnect market was, by early 2025, accreting demand at a pace few had anticipated two years earlier. The expansion of large-language-model training clusters required not only accelerated compute but dense, high-capacity optical transport between GPU pods, between data centres, and along the regional long-haul routes connecting them. Infinera's subsea and terrestrial product lines slotted directly into that demand profile.

Nokia indicated the combined optical and IP networking business — grouped under the Network Infrastructure segment — would be managed as an integrated go-to-market toward hyperscaler and cloud accounts. Analysts at [Light Reading](https://www.lightreading.com) and elsewhere noted that the Infinera deal gave Nokia a sales motion inside Amazon Web Services, Google and Meta that its legacy equipment business had never fully cultivated. Integration execution over the twelve months following the close would determine whether that relationship capital could be translated into contracted revenue at scale.

## SR Linux and the AI data centre routing opportunity

The more speculative, and potentially more valuable, dimension of Hotard's strategic posture concerned IP routing. Nokia's IP Networks division traced its lineage directly to the Bell Labs-originated router engineering organisation acquired when Nokia bought Alcatel-Lucent for approximately €14.8 billion ($15.6 billion) in January 2016. That acquisition gave Nokia a routing platform — built around the SR OS operating system and, more recently, the SR Linux data-centre fabric operating system — capable of competing with Cisco Systems, Juniper Networks and the Arista Networks platforms that had come to dominate hyperscaler switching and routing fabrics.

SR Linux is the instrument through which Nokia articulated its AI data centre routing ambition. Unlike SR OS, which was engineered for carrier edge and core environments, SR Linux was built as a disaggregated, container-native network operating system suited to the leaf-spine topologies that large-scale GPU clusters demand. Nokia confirmed a commercial deployment with Microsoft as one of its reference hyperscaler customers, a validation carrying considerable weight in a market where Arista's share of AI back-end fabric had become a recurring subject of analyst commentary.

The opportunity is structural. As the scale of AI training infrastructure expands — expressed in the hundreds of thousands of Nvidia H100 and H200 GPU nodes that the leading hyperscalers announced through 2024 and 2025 — the interconnect and routing requirements of those clusters become a distinct and large procurement category. Nokia's argument was that SR Linux, combined with the Infinera optical layer, could offer hyperscalers a single-vendor or close-to-single-vendor solution across the Layer 0-through-3 stack within the data centre and on the campus interconnect. Cisco and Juniper advanced similar arguments; Arista's strength lay in the switching layer. The differentiation Nokia pressed was in optical integration depth and in the carrier-grade software reliability inherited from decades of service-provider engineering at Bell Labs and its successors.

## Revenue trajectory and the recovery thesis

| Fiscal year | Revenue (€ bn) | Year-on-year change |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 21.9 | — |
| 2021 | 22.2 | +1.4% |
| 2022 | 24.9 | +12.2% |
| 2023 | 22.3 | −10.4% |
| 2024 | 19.7 | −11.7% |

*Source: [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)*

The revenue compression of 2023 and 2024 reflected two forces operating simultaneously. First, the normalisation of 5G capital expenditure after the exceptional cycle of 2021–2022. Second, the loss of certain operator contracts in India and portions of Southeast Asia to competitors including Ericsson and Samsung Networks. Nokia's management acknowledged under Lundmark that the Indian market had not produced the returns the company had targeted when it committed capacity to serve Reliance Jio and Airtel deployments.

Hotard's recovery thesis rested on a different revenue mix. AI data centre infrastructure — optical transport, IP routing fabric and the associated network management software — was posited as a faster-growing segment in which Nokia could expand revenue content per customer without depending on the cyclical carrier capex pattern that had whipsawed Mobile Networks. Nokia Technologies, the patent licensing division, contributed a reliable high-margin baseline, its royalty streams derived from a portfolio developed over decades of cellular standards work and largely insulated from the equipment market's cyclicality.

## Competitive position and the peer set

Nokia's competitive landscape in the AI data centre routing space differed substantially from its carrier market peer set. Ericsson, the principal rival in Mobile Networks, had no meaningful router franchise and was not a direct competitor in the IP Networks segment. The threats in data centre routing came instead from Cisco — whose NCS and 8000-series routers held strong carrier edge positions and whose Nexus switching line was embedded across many hyperscaler campuses — Juniper, Arista and, outside Western procurement channels, Huawei Technologies.

Arista's trajectory in AI networking was widely tracked by investors through 2024 and 2025, as the Santa Clara company reported accelerating revenue from both front-end and back-end AI cluster networking products. Nokia was pitching against Arista at scale while simultaneously integrating a large acquisition and installing a new chief executive. The execution risk was real and acknowledged in the analyst community. What Nokia possessed that Arista did not was the Alcatel-Lucent deep routing heritage and, after February 2025, a material optical capability that could be bundled into the same hyperscaler conversation — spanning wavelength division multiplexing capacity all the way to the routed IP layer above it.

## Strategic posture, 2026–2030

As of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, the Hotard era was approximately thirteen months old. The broad outlines of the strategic posture had been communicated, but the financial results that would validate or refute them remained, in large measure, ahead of Nokia. The integration of Infinera was the most immediate operational variable: delivering cost synergies, retaining design engineering talent concentrated at Infinera's San Jose and Allentown facilities, and converting hyperscaler access into contracted volume would define the Network Infrastructure segment's trajectory through the remainder of the decade.

Nokia's structural advantage was the breadth of portfolio — optical, routing, radio and software — assembled over thirty years of acquisitions stretching from the 1992 purchase of Technophone through to the Infinera close. Hotard's task was to make that breadth coherent to a set of customers, the AI hyperscalers, who had historically sourced each layer of their network from best-of-breed specialists. Whether Nokia could shift that procurement logic in its favour — and do so while managing the Mobile Networks decline through a still-uncertain carrier capex recovery — remained the central question of the era he had inherited from Espoo's fifth floor.

leadership.key_finding: Nokia Corporation's executive structure reflects the strategic transformation through 2024-2025 from Pekka Lundmark's CEO leadership (August 2020-March 2025) to Justin Hotard's CEO succession (April 2025-present). Hotard joined from Intel Corporation where he had been Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Data Center and AI Group; the strategic mandate has been the AI data centre opportunity development through the Network Infrastructure business group particularly the IP Networks routing portfolio plus the broader operational and strategic posture continuation. The executive team layers the new Hotard strategic leadership with CFO Marco Wirén (since January 2021), the business group leadership across Network Infrastructure (Federico Guillen), Mobile Networks (Tommi Uitto), Cloud and Network Services, and Nokia Technologies (the patent licensing business), and broad operational and technology leadership. The board is chaired by Sari Baldauf (since 2020, the principal long-tenured female CEO/board leadership in Finnish technology industry) and includes long-tenured directors plus recent additions calibrated to the AI data centre infrastructure customer category positioning.
